Project Title: Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Generate Three-Dimensional Tropical Cyclone Wind Analyses, Including Surface Wind Estimates
Project Goal: By developing and refining machine learning models to generate three-dimensional and surface tropical cyclone wind analyses from airborne and satellite observations, this project aims to address the critical lack of operational, observationally-based tropical cyclone wind analyses for forecasters to resolve persistent gaps in storm intensity and size estimation.
Research Keywords: Artificial Intelligence (AI) / Machine Learning (ML), Model & Forecast Guidance, Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP)
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Advanced Weather Interactive Processing System (AWIPS), Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS)
Project Description: This project refines two machine learning models, WHOMP and TC-SWARM, to deliver two-dimensional surface wind estimates and three-dimensional tropical cyclone wind analyses. WHOMP utilizes lower-tropospheric vertical wind profiles and environmental metrics to estimate surface winds, while TC-SWARM uses geostationary infrared satellite data and operational model analyses to generate full three-dimensional wind fields when aircraft reconnaissance is unavailable. Both capabilities will be transitioned into the operational AWIPS-II environment at the National Hurricane Center via the Hurricane and Ocean Testbed. In addition, the machine learning analyses will serve as an observational benchmark to diagnose structural and intensity biases in high-resolution HAFS numerical model forecasts.

Project Title: A Convection-allowing Ensemble System for Short-term Probabilistic Forecasts of Severe Convective Hazards Based on the MPAS Dynamic Core
Project Goal: Evaluate a MPAS-based data assimilation (DA) and prediction system in HWT and HMT experiments for short-term probabilistic guidance of severe thunderstorms. Migrate from the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) to Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) software, which will be the backbone of future operational convective-scale DA systems.
Research Keywords: Data Assimilation and Ensembles, Model & Forecast Guidance, Decision Support
Project Description: This project proposes the development and evaluation of a storm-scale ensemble data assimilation and prediction system based on the MPAS dynamic core and JEDI software for short-term probabilistic forecasts of severe convective hazards. It aims to provide improved guidance for severe thunderstorms and flash flooding by migrating the existing DA system from DART to JEDI, enhancing resolution to 1-km, and rigorous evaluation through Hazardous Weather Testbed (HWT) and Hydrometeorology Testbed (HMT) experiments.
Project Benefits: The probabilistic guidance products from the MPAS-based system will be used in NWS operations to increase lead-time and accuracy of watches and warnings for severe convective weather and extreme precipitation that leads to flash flooding. Depending on performance, this system could be a candidate to replace the WRF-based "Warn-on-Forecast System".

Project Title: Guidelines for Expressing Uncertainty in Impact Decision Support Service Products: Supplement to NSF award "Improving Public Response to Weather Warnings

Project Description: This project builds on base funding from NSF, in which the PI explores the ways forecast uncertainty is communicated as events unfold over time, and how the various options for conveying risk in time can affect judgments about risk. It may also include a list misinterpretations to guard against and how. It may provide guidance for how to deal with multiple hazard events. It will suggest procedures for identifying user needs and concerns and methods adapting communication techniques to meet them that can be applied to winter storms, heavy rain and heat events in the NOAA/NWS WFO Seattle and NOAA constituencies nationwide.

Project Title: An Examination of the State of Knowledge on Risk Perceptions and Understanding Response to Uncertainty Information
Project Goal: The major goal of this project was to conduct a multi-disciplinary meta-analysis on the public's response to uncertainty information.
Research Keywords: Communicating Probabilities & Uncertainty, Risk Communication, Risk Perception & Response, "Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences (SBES)"
Project Description: This project conducts a multi-disciplinary systematic review of the literature on uncertainty. The overarching research question is how does the general public respond to and interpret uncertainty?
Project Benefits: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and its affiliates have invested heavily in improving forecasting measures and making information available to the public. While several advancements have been made in measurement, atmospheric sensing, modeling, and other innovative developments, there is limited understanding about how the public responds to these products. Considerable attention has been given to the idea of changing how weather forecast information is shared with the public, especially regarding how forecast uncertainty is incorporated with additional probabilistic information. In contemplating the ways in which probabilistic information could impact the public, it is important to gain a baseline understanding of how decision-making is shaped by uncertainty.

Project Title: Estimating the Economic Benefits of the Tornado Warning Improvement and Extension Program
Project Goal: This project estimates the potential economic benefits of a Tornado Warning Improvement and Extension Program (TWIEP), especially on U.S. businesses and tornado-vulnerable populations.
Research Keywords: Economic Valuation, Social Vulnerability, "Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences (SBES)"
Project Description: In the recently-passed Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Act of 2017, Congress calls for improvements in tornado warning lead-times from the current average of 13 minutes (Erickson and Brooks 2006) to an hour (115 th Cong 2017). A program change of this magnitude would expand the behavioral response options of the populations in harm's way, which may be especially beneficial for reducing the mortality and morbidity rate of society's most vulnerable. Vulnerable populations are of particular interest because their injury and fatality rates far exceed those of other populations, and they may perish in many of the tornadoes that occur, not just the rarest and most intense tornadoes (Sutter and Simmons 2010). If vulnerable populations were to see an improved ability to access, understand, and respond to threats under this paradigm, part of the value of the TWIEP can be estimated based on the anticipated reduction in fatalities for these groups. In addition to the potential impacts for vulnerable populations, the TWIEP may also impact the decisions businesses make ahead of potential tornado threats. Specifically, the tornado warning improvements currently under development include the estimation of the likelihood that a storm may produce a given hazard, like a tornado (Rothfusz et al. 2018).
Project Benefits: The Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Act of 2017 requires NOAA to prioritize research to improve weather data, modeling, computing, forecasts, and warnings for the protection of life, property and the enhancement of the national economy. More specifically, the act calls for improvements in tornado warning lead-times from the current average of 13 minutes (Erickson and Brooks 2006) to an hour (115th Cong 2017). NOAA's Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR), Office of Weather and Air Quality is focusing on understanding the economic impact of an improved understanding of forecast capabilities for atmospheric events. This study is one such effort to focus on the value of 1-hour lead time. Since economic valuation is a multi-step process, this study provides foundational analysis in developing methodologies and an initial data set that will allow NOAA to understand the value of 1-hour lead time and the value of the research investments to reach that goal.

Project Title: A Web Based Survey to Estimate the Economic Value of Improved Hurricane Forecasts
Project Goal: The goal of this project was to evaluate the public's willingness to pay for more accurate hurricane forecasts through a large-scale choice experiment. Focusing on areas recently hit by hurricanes, this project establishes the value of improvements in storm track, wind speed, and precipitation forecast precision.
Research Keywords: Model & Forecast Guidance, Economic Valuation, "Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences (SBES)"
Project Description: The economic value of hurricane forecasts is directly related to its ability to affect behavior; namely household evacuation. Members of the public will complete a survey that varies the attributes of a hurricane forecast (e.g., storm surge, landfall location, intensity forecast) and possible mitigation behaviors (e.g., a monetary voucher to evacuate) in order to provide the time and/or expenditure costs of their choices. Overall, this project will estimate an overall value of improving hurricane forecasts.
Project Benefits: The Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Act of 2017 requires NOAA to prioritize research that improves forecasts and warnings for the protection of life, property, and the enhancement of the national economy. More specifically, targets improvements in hurricane forecasts that incorporate risk communication to create more effective watch and warning products (P.Law 115-25, Title 1, 101, 102, 104). As such, this research assesses the economic impact of improving hurricane forecasts and warnings through a public survey regarding how forecasts of varying precision affect human behavior. By manipulating forecast and behavioral attributes, this project will estimate an overall value of improving hurricane forecasts. Research on behavioral economics not only provides a value of improving a forecast, but may also help NOAA prioritize which attribute of an improved forecast will help NOAA meet its mission of protecting lives and property and, in turn, provide guidance on physical science research priorities.

Project Title: Joint Project: Social Media Message Amplification and Attentional Networks
Project Goal: The goal of this NSF-NOAA supplemental research was to identify factors that are predictive of message retransmission (i.e., amplification) of NWS messaging on social media.
Research Keywords: Flow of Weather Risk Information, "Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences (SBES)"
Project Description: Social Science Transitions from Research into Operations: a NOAA and NSF Grant project, called the STRONG project for short, is an innovative funding partnership between OWAQ and the National Science Foundation (NSF) that takes advantage of ongoing investments in basic research at NSF to hasten application at NOAA. This STRONG project uses machine learning to code the corpus of 12 NWS WFO tweets from 2013-2016 according to their engagement content (i.e., information, action, and community building) and structure (e.g., hashtags, URLs). These message variables will be used to predict which types of message content and message structure lead to amplification (i.e., passed on via retweeting) of NWS tweets during threat and non-threat periods. In addition, this study will explore the interoffice interactions among the 12 WFOs that also lead to message retransmission.
Project Benefits: This study has R2O communication implications by isolating how the NWS should communicate via social media during threat and non-threat periods in order to have their messages obtain the greatest amount of exposure.
